script:
Lena: Jake, we need to talk about the kitchen.
Jake: Oh no. Is it that bad?
Lena: Well, there are dirty dishes in the sink again, and it's your week to clean.
Jake: I'm sorry. I had a long day at work, and I forgot.
Lena: I understand, but I worked late too, and I still washed my cup.
Jake: You're right. How about I do the dishes now and take out the trash tomorrow morning?
Lena: That sounds fair. Maybe we can also make a list of chores and put it on the fridge.
Jake: Good idea. Then nobody has to remind anybody.
Lena: Thanks, Jake. I really appreciate it.

qs.q: What is Lena's complaint?
opts: There are dirty dishes in the sink
The trash is outside the door
qs.why: She says there are dirty dishes in the sink again.

qs.q: Why does Jake say he forgot?
opts: He had a long day at work
He didn't know it was his week
qs.why: Jake says he had a long day at work.

qs.q: What will they put on the fridge?
qs.why: Lena suggests making a list of chores and putting it on the fridge.

script:
Mia: Excuse me, Mr Collins. Do you have a minute?
Mr Collins: Of course, Mia. What's up?
Mia: I'd like to take next Friday off. My sister is getting married, and the wedding is on Saturday in Leeds.
Mr Collins: Congratulations to her! Friday is fine, but we have a team meeting that morning.
Mia: I know. I can send my report on Thursday, so nobody has to wait for me.
Mr Collins: That would be perfect. Please also ask Tom to help with any urgent emails.
Mia: Yes, I'll do that. Thank you so much.
Mr Collins: You're welcome. Enjoy the wedding.

qs.q: Why does Mia want Friday off?
opts: She wants to travel for her sister's wedding
She is moving to a new house
She needs to finish a report
qs.why: Her sister is getting married on Saturday in Leeds.

qs.q: What will Mia do before she leaves?
qs.why: She offers to send her report on Thursday.

qs.q: Who will help with urgent emails?
qs.why: Mr Collins asks Mia to ask Tom for help.

script: Every September, my town holds a food festival, and it's my favorite weekend of the year. The main street is closed to cars, and hundreds of people walk between the stalls. You can try dishes from many countries, like Mexican tacos, Indian curry, and Italian ice cream. Local families also sell homemade bread and cakes. There is live music in the park, and children can join free cooking classes. My advice is to arrive early, because the lines get long after noon. Also, bring some cash, since a few small stalls don't take cards. Last year I ate so much that I couldn't have dinner. This year I'm going to share dishes with my friends, so we can taste more things.

qs.q: When does the festival take place?
qs.why: The speaker says the festival is held every September.

qs.q: Why does the speaker suggest arriving early?
opts: The lines are long after noon
The food is free in the morning
qs.why: The lines get long after noon.

qs.q: Why should visitors bring cash?
opts: Some small stalls don't accept cards
The cooking classes are not free
There are no banks in town
qs.why: A few small stalls don't take cards.

script: Hello, this is Rachel from the fraud team at Northern Bank. I'm calling because we noticed an unusual payment on your card this morning. It was for four hundred pounds at an electronics shop in another city. If you made this payment, you don't need to do anything. If you didn't, please call the number on the back of your card as soon as you can, and we will block the card straight away. Please remember that we will never ask you to share your PIN or your full password, either by phone or by email. If anyone asks for that information, hang up. Thank you, and have a good day.

qs.q: Why is Rachel calling?
opts: To offer a new credit card
qs.why: The bank noticed an unusual payment on the card.

qs.q: What should the customer do if they didn't make the payment?
opts: Send an email with the PIN
Call the number on the back of the card
qs.why: Rachel says to call the number on the back of the card so the bank can block it.

qs.q: What will the bank never ask for?
qs.why: The bank will never ask customers to share their PIN or full password.

script:
Carlos: Dana, how do you study for the history exam so quickly?
Dana: I use an AI assistant to summarize my notes. It turns ten pages into one page.
Carlos: Isn't that risky? What if the summary has mistakes?
Dana: That's true. I always compare it with my textbook. It saves time, but I don't trust it completely.
Carlos: Does it also help you with writing essays?
Dana: It gives me ideas, but I write the essay myself. My teacher can tell when a student copies a text.
Carlos: Good point. Maybe I should try it for my notes.
Dana: Just check everything first. Honestly, that's the most important rule.

qs.q: How does Dana use the AI assistant?
qs.why: She says it turns ten pages of notes into one page.

qs.q: What does Dana do to avoid mistakes?
opts: She compares the summary with her textbook
qs.why: She says she always compares it with her textbook.

qs.q: What does Dana say about essays?
opts: AI writes them better than students
She writes them herself and only gets ideas from AI
qs.why: The AI gives her ideas, but she writes the essay herself.

script: Good evening, visitors, and welcome to the City Art Museum's late-night opening. Tonight, the museum will stay open until eleven o'clock, and entry to all galleries is free. On the second floor, a guide will give a short talk about our new photography exhibition at eight and again at nine thirty. In the main hall, a local band will play jazz from seven o'clock. Please remember that photographs are allowed, but flash photography is not. The café on the ground floor is open until ten, and the gift shop closes at nine. If you need any help, our staff are wearing green badges. We hope you enjoy your evening.

qs.q: What is special about tonight?
opts: The museum is open late and entry is free
qs.why: The museum stays open until eleven, and entry is free.

qs.q: What is not allowed in the museum?
qs.why: Photographs are allowed, but flash photography is not.

qs.q: What closes at nine o'clock?
qs.why: The gift shop closes at nine, while the café stays open until ten.

script: I've been working from home for two years, and I've learned a few things. First, have a fixed routine. I start at nine and finish at six, and I take a proper lunch break away from my desk. Second, create a separate workspace. When I worked on the sofa, I found it hard to switch off in the evening. Now I have a small desk in the corner of my bedroom, and I close my laptop when the day ends. Third, stay in touch with colleagues. I used to send only emails, but now I call people more often, and it makes teamwork easier. Of course, working from home isn't perfect, but these habits really help me stay productive and relaxed.

qs.q: What does the speaker do at lunchtime?
opts: Takes a break away from the desk
qs.why: He takes a proper lunch break away from his desk.

qs.q: Why did the speaker get a separate desk?
opts: It was hard to switch off in the evening
qs.why: When he worked on the sofa, he found it hard to switch off.

qs.q: What changed about his communication with colleagues?
qs.why: He used to send only emails, but now he calls people more often.

script:
Priya: Mike, did you get that email about the payroll update?
Mike: I did. It said I had to confirm my details through a link within twenty-four hours.
Priya: Exactly. I almost clicked, but the sender's address looked slightly odd. It had an extra letter in the company name.
Mike: Good catch. Those messages are designed to create panic, so people act before they think.
Priya: That's what worries me. Some of our newer colleagues might fall for it.
Mike: Then we should report it to the security team right away. They can warn everyone and block the sender.
Priya: Agreed. Should we forward it, or use the report button?
Mike: The report button. Forwarding it could spread the risk, and the button gives the team the technical details they need.

qs.q: What made Priya suspicious of the email?
opts: The sender's address had an extra letter
It came from the security team
qs.why: She noticed an extra letter in the company name in the address.

qs.q: Why do these messages usually include a short deadline?
opts: To make people act without thinking
To save time for the sender
qs.why: Mike says such messages are designed to create panic so people act before they think.

qs.q: What do Priya and Mike decide to do?
qs.why: Mike recommends the report button instead of forwarding, and Priya agrees.

script:
Hannah: Ross, I've looked at the schedule, and I'm afraid the launch date isn't realistic.
Ross: That's a problem. The client expects the final version by the end of the month.
Hannah: I know, but two of our developers are off sick, and the testing phase will take longer than planned.
Ross: Could we deliver the core features first and add the rest later?
Hannah: That might work. If we focus on the essentials, we could meet the original deadline with a slightly smaller product.
Ross: I'd have to check whether the client agrees to that.
Hannah: Of course. I'll prepare a short summary showing what we can deliver and what would be delayed.
Ross: Perfect. Send it by lunchtime, and I'll call them this afternoon.

qs.q: Why is the launch date unrealistic?
opts: Two developers are sick and testing will take longer
qs.why: Hannah mentions two developers off sick and a longer testing phase.

qs.q: What does Ross suggest?
opts: Moving the deadline to next year
qs.why: He asks whether they could deliver the core features first and add the rest later.

qs.q: What will Hannah do next?
opts: Prepare a summary of what can and can't be delivered
qs.why: She will prepare a short summary and send it by lunchtime.

script: My closest friend moved abroad five years ago, and I was afraid we would drift apart. At first, we tried to talk every day, but time zones made that exhausting, and we both felt guilty when we missed a call. Eventually, we changed our approach. Now we send short voice messages whenever something funny or important happens, and we answer when we have time. Once a month, we schedule a proper video call. Surprisingly, our friendship feels stronger than before, because we share more honest details of our lives. I've realized that closeness isn't about talking constantly. It's about making the effort to stay interested in each other, even from a distance.

qs.q: Why was daily contact difficult at first?
qs.why: Time zones made daily calls exhausting, and they felt guilty about missed calls.

qs.q: How do the friends stay in touch now?
opts: With voice messages and a monthly video call
By visiting each other every month
qs.why: They send voice messages and schedule one video call a month.

qs.q: What is the speaker's main point?
opts: Closeness comes from effort and interest, not constant contact
qs.why: She says closeness is about making the effort to stay interested, not talking constantly.

script: Education officials have published new guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence in secondary schools. Rather than banning the tools outright, the guidelines ask schools to set clear rules about when students may use them. Teachers will be encouraged to design assignments that require personal reflection, which is harder to generate automatically. Schools will also be asked to teach pupils how to check information and recognise errors in AI-generated answers. Supporters say this approach prepares young people for the modern workplace. Critics, however, worry that some students will still rely on the technology too heavily and neglect basic writing skills. The guidelines will be reviewed again at the end of the next academic year.

qs.q: What approach do the guidelines take?
opts: Clear rules about when AI may be used
Free use of AI at all times
qs.why: Schools are asked to set clear rules rather than ban the tools outright.

qs.q: Why are assignments requiring personal reflection encouraged?
opts: They are harder to generate automatically
qs.why: Personal reflection is harder to generate automatically.

qs.q: What is the critics' concern?
opts: Students may neglect basic writing skills
Schools will not have enough computers
qs.why: Critics worry that some students will rely on the technology too heavily and neglect writing skills.

script:
Nick: I can't believe you watch foreign films with dubbing. You lose the actors' real voices.
Emma: But if I'm reading subtitles, I miss half of what's happening on screen.
Nick: That's only because you're not used to it. After a few films, your eyes adapt.
Emma: Maybe, but dubbing lets me relax after a long day. Besides, some dubbed versions are excellent.
Nick: Sure, but the jokes rarely translate well. A phrase can lose its whole meaning.
Emma: Fair point. Perhaps I'm being lazy.
Nick: Not lazy, just comfortable. Why don't we watch the next one with subtitles, and you can judge for yourself?
Emma: Deal. But if I hate it, we're going back to dubbing.

qs.q: Why does Nick prefer subtitles?
opts: They keep the actors' real voices
qs.why: He says dubbing makes you lose the actors' real voices.

qs.q: What is Emma's objection to subtitles?
opts: She misses what is happening on screen
qs.why: She says she misses half of what's happening on screen.

qs.q: What do they agree to do?
opts: Watch the next film with subtitles
qs.why: Emma accepts Nick's suggestion to try subtitles for the next film.

script: Cybersecurity experts are reminding travellers to be careful when using public Wi-Fi networks in airports, cafés and hotels. These networks are often open, which means other users on the same connection may be able to intercept unprotected data. Experts recommend avoiding online banking or shopping on a public network unless you use a virtual private network, known as a VPN, which encrypts your traffic. They also advise checking the exact name of the network with staff, because criminals sometimes create fake hotspots with similar names. Finally, travellers should keep their phone and laptop software up to date, since updates often fix known security weaknesses. Using your mobile data instead is usually a safer choice for sensitive tasks.

qs.q: Why can public Wi-Fi be risky?
opts: Other users may intercept unprotected data
qs.why: Open networks may let other users intercept unprotected data.

qs.q: Why should travellers check the network name with staff?
opts: To avoid paying for the service
To avoid fake hotspots with similar names
qs.why: Criminals sometimes create fake hotspots with similar names.

qs.q: What does a VPN do, according to the report?
qs.why: The report says a VPN encrypts your traffic.

script: For years, I wore my exhaustion like a badge of honor. I answered emails at midnight, skipped vacations, and believed that being constantly available proved my commitment. Then, one winter, I realized I could no longer concentrate, and small tasks felt overwhelming. It turned out to be burnout, and recovering took months. What surprised me most was how little my absence disrupted the team. The work continued, and my colleagues managed perfectly well. Since returning, I've set firm boundaries: I switch off notifications after six, I take my full vacation, and I say no to projects that I can't realistically finish. Ironically, my performance has improved. I've come to see rest not as a reward for productivity, but as a prerequisite for it.

qs.q: What did the speaker used to believe?
opts: Rest is a waste of time
qs.why: He believed that being constantly available proved his commitment.

qs.q: What surprised the speaker most?
opts: The team managed well without him
qs.why: He was surprised how little his absence disrupted the team.

qs.q: What conclusion does the speaker reach?
opts: Rest is a reward for good results
Rest is a requirement for productivity
qs.why: He sees rest as a prerequisite for productivity, not a reward.

script:
Nora: I need your advice about Claire. She's cancelled on me three times this month, and each time the excuse sounds a bit thin.
Ben: Have you told her how that makes you feel?
Nora: Not really. I don't want to seem needy, and I'm afraid of starting an argument over something trivial.
Ben: But it clearly isn't trivial if it's bothering you this much. Resentment tends to build quietly until it comes out in an argument.
Nora: True. Still, what if she's going through something difficult and hasn't told me?
Ben: Then asking her directly gives her the chance to open up. You could say you've missed her instead of accusing her of anything.
Nora: That's a much gentler way to put it. I'll message her tonight and suggest a coffee.
Ben: Good. And whatever she says, listen before you respond.

qs.q: What is bothering Nora?
opts: Claire has cancelled plans three times this month
qs.why: Nora says Claire has cancelled on her three times this month.

qs.q: Why hasn't Nora spoken to Claire about it?
opts: She doesn't want to seem needy or start an argument
She has already spoken to her
qs.why: She doesn't want to seem needy and fears an argument over something trivial.

qs.q: What does Ben suggest?
opts: Saying she has missed Claire instead of accusing her
qs.why: He suggests saying she's missed her rather than accusing her of anything.
